chapter_title: Distance and Motion Sensors: Ultrasonic and PIR

screens.title: Distance & Motion Sensors: Ultrasonic and PIR
screens.subtitle: Measure how far, detect when someone moves, and combine the two for responsive projects.

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn two common sensors for making Arduino projects aware of the world: the HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor and the PIR motion sensor. You'll see how the ultrasonic sensor sends a short sound pulse and measures the time until an echo returns, and how that time converts to a physical distance. You'll also learn how a PIR sensor senses changes in infrared energy to report motion and how its sensitivity and output timing are adjusted on the module. Together these sensors let you build practical projects like a parking aid that only activates when a person is present, or a light that turns on for people within a certain range. The chapter emphasizes wiring the sensor pins, the trigger and echo timing detail for the ultrasonic module, the simple digital read model for PIR, and a short hands-on activity that combines both sensors to change beep rate based on distance. By the end you'll understand the core signal types, the timing concept that turns echo duration into centimeters, and typical limitations to watch for in real environments.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Ultrasonic sensors measure distance by timing sound echoes; PIR sensors detect motion by sensing changes in infrared energy. Combining timing and digital signals creates responsive systems.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll gain and why they matter

narration.text: Over the next screens you'll learn four concrete Arduino skills tied to ultrasonic and PIR sensors. First, you'll measure distance with the HC-SR04 by producing a short trigger pulse and timing the echo; this matters because timing converts directly into distance measurements that you can use for control. Second, you'll detect motion with a PIR sensor and learn how its output behaves when a warm body moves in front of it; that lets you create presence-aware systems that activate only when needed. Third, you'll combine sensor data to design interactions — for example, enabling distance checks only after motion is detected — which reduces false alarms and saves power. Fourth, you'll understand timing, trigger and echo concepts well enough to troubleshoot noisy readings and to compute the correct conversion factor from microseconds to centimeters. Each objective includes a small visual mnemonic to help you remember the signal type and a milestone you can check by building the parking sensor activity at the end.

screens.title: How the HC-SR04 Ultrasonic Sensor Works
screens.subtitle: Trigger, echo, and converting time to distance

narration.text: The HC-SR04 measures distance by sending a short burst of high-frequency sound and waiting for an echo. Concretely, you create a tiny trigger pulse to tell the sensor to transmit ultrasonic pulses; the sensor then sets its echo pin HIGH for the duration between emission and return. That duration is proportional to the round-trip travel time of sound. To compute distance you multiply the measured time by the speed of sound and divide by two to account for the journey there and back. For example, the lesson text gives the conversion factor 0.034, which is the speed of sound expressed in centimeters per microsecond. Multiply the echo duration by 0.034 and then divide by two to get centimeters. A common misconception is to forget dividing by two — that yields double the actual distance, so always account for the round trip. Accuracy depends on stable timing and clear echoes; soft or angled surfaces produce weaker returns and may give noisy durations. Concrete example: if the echo lasts one thousand microseconds, applying the formula gives about seventeen centimeters. Practice sending the standard 10-microsecond trigger and reading the echo duration repeatedly to get stable readings; averaging multiple measurements reduces noise. Reflect: how would echoes from multiple surfaces affect the reading, and how can repeated samples help?

keyIdea.title: Distance by timing
keyIdea.text: Ultrasonic sensors time a sound pulse's round trip; convert microseconds to distance using the speed of sound and divide by two for the return journey.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › HC-SR04 Basics
Definition
Ultrasonic distance by echo timing
The sensor emits pulses and raises the echo pin for the time it takes sound to travel to an object and return. Timing is the measurement; math converts it to centimeters.
Key points
  • Send a short trigger pulse to start emission.
  • Measure echo pin HIGH duration in microseconds.
  • Distance = duration × 0.034 ÷ 2 (centimeters).
Common misconception
If you forget to divide by two you report double the distance. Weak echoes from soft materials can produce noisy or missing readings.
Visual: code & formula
Example sketch (visual only; use the serial monitor to verify readings)
const int trigPin = 9;
const int echoPin = 10;

// trigger, measure echo, convert to cm
// duration * 0.034 / 2 = distance in cm
Example
An echo duration of 1000 microseconds becomes 1000 × 0.034 ÷ 2 ≈ 17 cm. Repeat measurements and average for stability.
Key Takeaway
Timing is the measurement. Convert microseconds into distance with the speed of sound and the round-trip correction.

screens.title: Wiring and Trigger/Echo Sequence
screens.subtitle: Pins, pulses, and the microsecond timing sequence

narration.text: Getting reliable distance readings starts with correct wiring and a precise trigger sequence. The HC-SR04 module exposes four pins: VCC for power, Trig for the trigger input, Echo for the output pulse, and GND for ground. You power VCC from the Arduino's five volts and connect GND to ground. Attach the Trig pin to a digital output and Echo to a digital input capable of timing pulses. The typical sequence is simple but timing-sensitive: first set the trigger pin LOW for a short stabilization, then write a HIGH pulse of ten microseconds, then set it LOW again. Immediately measure the duration of the Echo pin while it is HIGH; that duration is in microseconds. Use a function that measures pulse length reliably. A common pitfall is to use long delays instead of microsecond delays around the trigger; microsecond precision matters because the conversion factor assumes microsecond timing. Another practical trick is to allow a small delay between successive measurements to let echoes settle and to avoid overlapping pulses. Example practice: wire trig to pin nine, echo to pin ten, and produce a 10-microsecond pulse before calling the pulse read routine. Reflect: if you get noisy results, check wiring, ensure the sensor has a clear path to the object, and add brief pauses between reads to avoid pulse interference.

keyIdea.title: Sequence matters
keyIdea.text: Correct wiring and a precise microsecond trigger pulse produce the echo duration you convert into distance; timing precision is essential.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Wiring & Trigger Sequence
Wiring
  • VCC → 5V, GND → GND
  • Trig → Digital output (e.g., pin 9)
  • Echo → Digital input (e.g., pin 10) to measure pulse duration
Use stable power and short wiring to reduce noise.
Trigger sequence
Stabilize LOW, pulse HIGH for 10 microseconds, then measure Echo pulse duration in microseconds.
Process steps
1. Ensure sensor has power and ground. 2. Set trigger LOW then HIGH for ten microseconds. 3. Read the echo duration with a pulse measurement. 4. Convert to centimeters using the conversion factor.
Example wiring note
If the echo pin remains LOW, confirm the Trig pulse timing and that Echo is connected to the input pin able to be read by your timing function.
Pitfall
Using long delays around the trigger can distort timing precision. Use microsecond delays for trigger timing.

screens.title: Reading Echo with pulseIn() — Example Sketch
screens.subtitle: Understand what each part of the example does and why

narration.text: Let's walk through the example sketch that many learners use to measure distance. The program defines pins for trigger and echo and configures serial output so you can see measurements. In the setup you set the trigger pin as an output and the echo pin as an input. The loop begins by stabilizing the trigger low, waiting two microseconds, then sending a ten-microsecond HIGH pulse to the trigger pin; this instructs the sensor to emit ultrasonic bursts. Immediately after the trigger, the code calls a function to measure how long the echo pin stays HIGH. That duration is returned in microseconds. The sketch then applies the conversion factor — the duration multiplied by 0.034 and divided by two — to produce a distance in centimeters and prints that value on the serial monitor. A practical tip is to insert a short delay between loop iterations so echoes from previous pulses clear and the sensor has time to settle. A common misconception is to expect perfect readings on the first try; instead, expect noise and use repeated readings or averaging to smooth results. For troubleshooting, observe the serial output: long or zero durations suggest wiring or obstruction issues. Reflect: how might you adapt the sketch to skip readings when the PIR indicates no motion?

screens.title: Speed of Sound and the Distance Formula
screens.subtitle: Why we multiply duration by 0.034 and divide by two

narration.text: The conversion from echo duration to distance relies on the speed of sound. The chapter gives a factor of 0.034, which expresses sound speed in centimeters per microsecond. Multiplying the measured duration by this factor yields the round-trip distance. Because the echo time includes the trip to the object and the return trip, you must divide by two to obtain the one-way distance between sensor and object. A two-part misconception often appears: either forgetting the divide-by-two step or applying an incorrect speed factor. Use the exact factor provided in the source to stay consistent. The practical limits of the sensor — about two centimeters to four hundred centimeters — come from how strong the echo is and the module's internal timing. Very close distances near the two-centimeter lower limit may not return reliable echoes, and long distances approach the limits of sensitivity, so readings can be noisy. Example calculation: an echo lasting one thousand microseconds becomes 1000 times 0.034 divided by two, roughly seventeen centimeters. If you average multiple durations and discard obviously impossible values, you reduce the impact of spurious echoes from angled or soft surfaces. Consider: what filtering strategy would you use to ignore one-off outliers in a stream of measurements?

keyIdea.title: Formula clarity
keyIdea.text: Distance in centimeters equals echo duration times 0.034 divided by two; the divide-by-two corrects for the round-trip travel of sound.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Speed of Sound & Formula
Why 0.034?
The chapter provides 0.034 as the speed of sound in centimeters per microsecond. Multiply duration by this factor, then divide by two to correct for the round trip.
Quick example
Echo duration 1000 microseconds → 1000 × 0.034 ÷ 2 ≈ 17 cm.
Limitations
The sensor can measure roughly from 2 cm to 400 cm. Soft or angled surfaces weaken echoes, and readings degrade at extremes.
Practical filtering
  • Take several readings and compute an average.
  • Discard zero or clearly out-of-range values before averaging.
  • Use brief pauses between triggers to avoid overlapping echoes.
Key Takeaway
Use the provided factor and the round-trip correction, and apply simple filtering to improve measurement reliability.

screens.title: PIR Sensor Principles
screens.subtitle: How Passive Infrared sensors detect motion

narration.text: A PIR sensor detects motion by sensing changes in infrared radiation in its field of view. Warm bodies like humans and animals emit infrared energy; when that pattern changes — for example when someone walks into the sensor's detection zone — the PIR's internal electronics detect the change and set the output pin HIGH. The module itself usually includes two adjustable controls: one for sensitivity and one for how long the output stays HIGH after detection. Wiring is simple: the PIR module typically has three pins — VCC, OUT, and GND. Connect VCC to power, OUT to a digital input, and GND to ground. In code you simply read the digital input; if it's HIGH, motion has been detected. Because the module holds the output HIGH for a configurable time, you often don't need debouncing in software: the hardware already smooths short fluctuations. A common misconception is to expect PIR to measure exact position or distance — it only reports a change in infrared energy, not a precise location. Concrete example: connect the PIR output to a digital pin and light an LED while the pin remains HIGH. Reflect: how would you tune sensitivity and time controls if your circuit triggers from pets but you only want human detection?

keyIdea.title: PIR summary
keyIdea.text: PIR modules detect changes in infrared energy and provide a simple digital HIGH output when motion is present; sensitivity and hold time are adjustable on the module.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › PIR Principles
How PIR works
PIR senses changes in infrared radiation. When the pattern changes, the module's output pin goes HIGH for a configurable period.
Wiring
VCC → 5V, GND → GND, OUT → digital input. Read the output with a simple digitalRead to detect motion.
Module adjustments
Two potentiometers adjust sensitivity and the duration the output stays HIGH. Use these to tune behavior for your environment.
Concrete example
Connect the PIR output to a digital pin and an LED to show detection. When the PIR reports HIGH, light the LED; when it reads LOW, turn the LED off. The module holds the signal HIGH for the configured time.
Key Takeaway
PIR provides a single, easy-to-read digital signal when motion occurs. Tune sensitivity and time to match your use case.

screens.title: Ultrasonic vs PIR: Strengths and Limitations
screens.subtitle: When to use distance sensing vs motion detection

narration.text: Ultrasonic and PIR sensors are complementary but serve different purposes. The ultrasonic HC-SR04 returns a measurable distance in centimeters, so you can detect how far an object is. It is best when you need quantitative range data — for example to modulate buzzer speed as an object approaches. However, ultrasonic sensors rely on clear echoes; soft, angled, or absorbent surfaces weaken the return, and accuracy declines at the extremes of the 2 to 400 centimeter range. PIR sensors, by contrast, detect a change in infrared energy and therefore indicate presence or movement rather than precise distance. They are useful for low-power wake-up signals or presence detection but cannot tell you how far a person is. A common mistake is to try to use a PIR where you need a distance measurement. Instead, use PIR to gate the more expensive or frequent distance checks from the ultrasonic sensor: only measure distance when the PIR indicates motion. This reduces false readings, saves processing and power, and produces a robust interaction. Example scenario: a parking aid uses HC-SR04 to measure how close a car is and a PIR to only run the distance checks when a person is in the car or nearby. Reflect: how would sensor placement influence false triggers for both sensors?

keyIdea.title: Use the right tool
keyIdea.text: Ultrasonic gives numerical distance; PIR gives presence. Combine them to get both efficiency and detail in interactions.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Ultrasonic vs PIR
Comparison
Ultrasonic
Provides distance in centimeters; relies on echo strength; sensitive to surface material and angle.
PIR
Indicates motion presence via infrared changes; configurable hold time and sensitivity; not a distance sensor.
Common mistake
Expecting PIR to replace an ultrasonic distance measurement. Use PIR for presence gating, not for measuring centimeters.
Concrete scenario
Parking sensor: PIR detects a person or approach, enabling the ultrasonic sensor to run distance checks only while someone is present, reducing false alarms and activity when no one is nearby.
Key Takeaway
Choose sensors by the information they provide; combine them to complement strengths and mitigate limitations.

screens.title: Designing a Combined Sensor System
screens.subtitle: Logic to gate distance checks with motion detection

narration.text: Designing systems that use both PIR and ultrasonic sensors is about controlling when you measure and how you react. Start by using the PIR sensor as a gate: if the PIR output is LOW, skip distance measurements to conserve cycles and avoid false triggers. When the PIR output goes HIGH, enable periodic ultrasonic measurements. Within the enabled state, trigger the ultrasonic sensor, measure echo duration, convert to distance, and then act — for example change beep rate or switch an LED. A practical control flow uses short loops: check PIR, if HIGH perform a distance measurement and map distance to an output behavior, then delay briefly before repeating. Consider also the PIR's hold time: the module may keep the output HIGH for a short period after movement, so you might still get distance reads even if motion has ceased momentarily. A common pitfall is running ultrasonic measurements at high frequency while motion is not present; this can create unnecessary noise and power use. Example: implement logic where the buzzer increases beep frequency as measured distance decreases, but only when PIR indicates presence. Reflect: how would you tune measurement intervals and PIR sensitivity to balance responsiveness and stability in a real environment?

keyIdea.title: Gating pattern
keyIdea.text: Use PIR to gate ultrasonic measurements: measure distance only when motion is present, then map distance to an action like buzzer speed.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Design: Combine Sensors
Flow outline
1. Read PIR output. 2. If PIR LOW, do nothing (sleep or wait). 3. If PIR HIGH, trigger ultrasonic sensor. 4. Read echo duration and convert to distance. 5. Map distance to output (buzzer rate, LED intensity).
Example mapping
Distance < 20 cm → fast beeps; 20–50 cm → slower beeps; >50 cm → silence.
Timing trade-offs
Short intervals make the system responsive but increase noise and power use. Use the PIR hold time to avoid unnecessary frequent distance reads.
Concrete scenario
A parking sensor runs only when the PIR sees motion near the vehicle. While enabled, the ultrasonic sensor measures distance and adjusts beep frequency as the car approaches a barrier.
Key Takeaway
Gating measurements with PIR reduces unnecessary work and improves reliability; map distance readings to clear output behaviors for the user to interpret.

screens.title: Build a Parking Sensor — Step-by-step
screens.subtitle: Use HC-SR04 to measure distance and make a buzzer beep faster as an object approaches

narration.text: The hands-on parking sensor is a focused project that highlights distance-to-action mapping. Begin by wiring the ultrasonic sensor to your Arduino: VCC to five volts, GND to ground, Trig to a digital output and Echo to a digital input. Add a piezo buzzer to a digital output pin. In the main loop, trigger the ultrasonic sensor, read the echo duration, convert it into centimeters using the chapter's formula, and then map that distance to a beep interval for the buzzer. A simple mapping is to set faster beeps when the distance is smaller and stop beeping when the object is farther than a threshold. A common practical tip is to clamp and validate distance results: ignore zero or extremely large values because they indicate no echo or an invalid reading. Also add a small delay between triggers to keep readings stable. Example mapping: under 20 centimeters produce rapid beeps; between 20 and 50 centimeters produce slower beeps; over 50 centimeters remain silent. Test with a stationary object and then with a moving object to ensure the beep rate changes smoothly. Reflect: how would you incorporate a PIR sensor so the buzzer sounds only when a person is present?

keyIdea.title: Activity snapshot
keyIdea.text: Trigger, measure, convert, and map distance to buzzer behavior. Validate and clamp readings to avoid false alerts.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Parking Sensor Activity
Activity steps
  1. Wire ultrasonic sensor and buzzer to Arduino.
  2. Trigger sensor, read echo duration, convert to cm.
  3. Map distance ranges to buzzer intervals.
  4. Validate readings and test with moving objects.
Validation rules
Discard zero or out-of-range values. Average multiple reads for smoother beep transitions.
Concrete mapping example
Distance < 20 cm → 100 ms beep interval. 20–50 cm → 400 ms interval. > 50 cm → silent. Tune ranges to match your vehicle and environment.
Key Takeaway
Map measured distance to a clear, perceivable behavior and validate readings to reduce false alerts.

screens.title: Adding PIR to the Parking Sensor
screens.subtitle: Use PIR to activate the system only when motion is present

narration.text: Incorporating a PIR sensor makes the parking sensor more context-aware and reduces unnecessary activity. Wire the PIR's VCC and GND to power and ground, and connect OUT to a digital pin on the Arduino. In your main loop, read the PIR pin first. If the PIR reads LOW, skip ultrasonic triggers and keep the buzzer silent. When the PIR reads HIGH, enable the distance measurement sequence and map distance to buzzer intervals as before. Because the PIR module holds its output HIGH for a configurable time, you may get a small window where the ultrasonic measurements continue after motion stops; tune the PIR's hold time potentiometer to match how long you want the system active. A common misconception is that the PIR will reliably detect all motion; small or slow movements may not trigger it depending on sensitivity settings. Test the combined system in the real parking environment: adjust sensor placement so the PIR sees approaching people and the ultrasonic sensor faces obstacles you intend to measure. Example: the PIR prevents the buzzer from sounding when the area is empty but allows the buzzer to warn when someone is present and a car approaches too close. Reflect: how might you add a visual indicator to show when the PIR has gated the ultrasonic sensor on?

keyIdea.title: Integration tip
keyIdea.text: PIR acts as a wake/gate for ultrasonic distance reads, reducing false alarms and unnecessary measurements when no motion is present.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Add PIR Gate
Integration steps
  • Wire PIR OUT to a digital input.
  • In the loop, read PIR first and skip ultrasonic if LOW.
  • When PIR HIGH, perform distance measurement and act.
Tuning
Adjust the PIR hold time to decide how long the ultrasonic sensor keeps measuring after the last detected motion.
Concrete example
PIR LOW → idle. PIR HIGH → measure distance; if distance < 20 cm, sound fast buzzer. Use an LED to indicate the PIR-gated active state for debugging and user feedback.
Key Takeaway
Gating distance reads with PIR improves responsiveness and reduces unnecessary sensing when the area is empty.

screens.title: Common Issues, Troubleshooting, and Assessment
screens.subtitle: How to interpret bad readings and the assessment question

narration.text: When you build sensor projects you will encounter noisy readings and occasional failures; knowing how to troubleshoot helps you find and fix problems quickly. If the ultrasonic echo duration reads zero, check that the echo pin is wired to the correct input and that you're sending the trigger pulse with microsecond precision. If readings jump or vary widely, try averaging several measurements and discarding zeros and out-of-range values before using the distance. Soft or angled surfaces can produce weak echoes; test with a flat, reflective target to verify the sensor's basic behavior. For PIR problems, if the sensor never reports HIGH, verify power and ground, ensure the module has warmed up, and check the sensitivity potentiometer. If it triggers too often, reduce sensitivity or change placement to avoid heat sources. For assessment practice, use the supplied calculation: if the Echo pulse lasts 1000 microseconds, what is the distance? Apply duration × 0.034 ÷ 2 to get approximately 17 centimeters. A final reflection question: when combining sensors, how do you balance responsiveness with false-trigger rejection in your code logic? Answering this helps you design stable, real-world interactions.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshoot checklist
keyIdea.text: Verify wiring, use microsecond trigger timing, validate and average measurements, and tune PIR sensitivity to reduce false triggers.

content.html:

Troubleshooting steps
  • Check wiring of Trig and Echo pins and ensure correct pinMode settings.
  • Use microsecond timing for trigger pulses and brief pauses between measurements.
  • Average multiple readings and discard zeros before using distance values.
  • Tune PIR sensitivity and hold time to reduce false positives.
Assessment idea
If Echo pulse = 1000 microseconds, distance = 1000 × 0.034 ÷ 2 ≈ 17 cm. This verifies you can apply the conversion correctly.
Concrete example
If readings fluctuate, log several values to the serial monitor, compute the average of valid samples, and use that averaged value to decide buzzer behavior. This reduces flicker and false alarms.
Key Takeaway
Measure carefully, validate readings, and tune hardware settings. Clear tests with known distances help confirm expected sensor behavior.

narration.text: Let's recap three essential ideas to carry forward. First, the HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor measures distance by timing the round-trip echo; convert microseconds to centimeters using the speed-of-sound factor and divide by two for the return trip. Second, pulseIn or an equivalent timing function returns the echo duration; ensure your trigger uses microsecond timing to get accurate measurements. Third, PIR sensors give a simple digital HIGH when they detect a change in infrared energy; use the module's sensitivity and hold-time controls to match the environment. Each of these ideas supports practical design decisions: use correct timing and conversion for ultrasonic distance, read and validate durations in code, and use PIR to gate or filter when you perform frequent measurements. Test these concepts with small experiments: verify the formula with a known distance, observe PIR behavior with different movements, and combine both sensors to see how they complement one another.

keyIdea.title: Memory aid
keyIdea.text: Timing + conversion = distance; PIR = presence signal; use PIR to reduce unnecessary distance checks.

narration.text: Finish with three practical reminders. First, validate and filter sensor data: ignore zeros and out-of-range values, average multiple readings, and pause briefly between triggers to avoid overlapping echoes. Second, be mindful of real-world limitations: accuracy decreases at very short or very long ranges, and surface properties affect ultrasonic echoes. Third, design combining logic to reduce false positives: use PIR as a gate to control when you perform more expensive distance reads. These reminders guide reliable project behavior: test in the intended environment, tune module adjustments, and prefer simple mappings from sensor values to actions that are easy for users to interpret. As you build, ask yourself whether a measurement is precise enough for the intended action and whether an additional sensor or a change in placement would improve performance. What to Remember (Part 2) means filter data, respect sensor limits, and combine sensors thoughtfully to produce stable, user-friendly behaviors.. In practical terms, final three memory cards. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
